nameStory: Water purslane gets its name from its love of wet places and its resemblance to common purslane, though the two aren't closely related. The 'water' part is a dead giveaway about where you'll find this plant - it's practically amphibious! Its scientific name Ludwigia palustris doubles down on this theme, with 'palustris' meaning 'of the marsh' in Latin.
description: Water purslane is a low-growing perennial herb that lives life on the water's edge. This sprawling plant forms mats of reddish stems that can grow both floating on water surfaces and creeping along muddy shores. Its small, oval leaves are arranged in opposite pairs along the stems, and the whole plant rarely gets taller than a few inches, preferring to spread outward rather than upward.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small oval leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem, smooth-edged and often with a waxy feel when you rub them between your fingers

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug wet ground or float on water surfaces, with stems that feel soft and succulent to the touch

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny greenish flowers tucked into leaf joints with no petals - easy to miss unless you look closely at the stem where leaves attach

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Reddish to green stems that are smooth, soft, and often have a slightly squishy texture when gently squeezed

habitat: Look for water purslane in marshes, pond edges, muddy streambanks, and seasonally flooded areas throughout New England. It thrives in spots that stay wet most of the year, from sea level wetlands to mountain bog margins. You'll often find it mixed with sedges, cattails, and other water-loving plants in areas that might be underwater in spring but just muddy by late summer.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as small reddish shoots from muddy substrates, often while areas are still partially flooded from snowmelt.
seasonality.summer: Plants form their characteristic spreading mats with full foliage, and tiny flowers appear tucked into leaf joints from June through August.
seasonality.fall: Stems and leaves often turn more distinctly reddish as temperatures cool, making the plant more noticeable against brown marsh vegetation.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back in most of New England, leaving only roots and seeds to survive until spring in protected muddy substrates.

funFact: Despite being called 'purslane,' this little marsh dweller is actually in the evening primrose family - making it a distant cousin of showy wildflowers like fireweed, rather than the succulent garden purslane you might toss in a salad!
confusionNotes: Water purslane is most easily confused with common purslane, but remember the habitat rule: if it's growing in water or very wet mud, it's likely water purslane, while common purslane prefers drier disturbed soils. Water purslane also has a more delicate, less fleshy appearance than its chunkier garden cousin.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'purslane' causes confusion because water purslane belongs to the evening primrose family, while common purslane is in the purslane family (Portulacaceae). They're completely unrelated plants that just happen to share a common name due to their similar low, spreading growth habits.
compareHints: Water purslane differs from its Ludwigia relatives like seedbox and globefruit primrose-willow by its tiny, inconspicuous flowers and low, mat-forming growth habit. While seedbox grows upright to several feet tall with showy yellow flowers, water purslane stays close to the ground with flowers so small you need to hunt for them. Think of it as the wallflower of the primrose-willow family.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Seedbox stands out from its primrose-willow relatives by its cube-shaped fruits and alternate leaves - water purslane has opposite leaves and tiny flowers, while globefruit primrose-willow has round (not square) seed pods.
Unlike its relative water purslane which has alternate leaves and tiny green flowers, globefruit primrose-willow has opposite leaves and yellow flowers.
